extracted.intended_audience: students, journalists, and general readers interested in broadcast journalism
extracted.subtask_description: A broad encyclopedia-style overview of broadcast journalism covering history, formats (radio, television, cable, online), newsroom roles, production practices, ethical standards, regulation, and education. Useful as a compendium of norms and standards for producing and evaluating broadcast news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing style — Five Ws and inverted pyramid
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing style (Five Ws · Inverted pyramid).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcast news writing follows classic newswriting rules: answer who/what/when/where/why/how (Five Ws) and often use the inverted pyramid structure to present the most important information first.

rubrics_metrics.name: News values (newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: News values (Above the fold · Man bites dog).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories should be evaluated for newsworthiness using conventional news values (e.g., prominence, timeliness, impact, novelty — 'man bites dog' — and placement priority such as 'above the fold').

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity and avoidance of false balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectivity; Media bias (False balance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcasts should aim for objective reporting while avoiding false balance (presenting two sides as equivalent when evidence does not warrant it); be aware of media bias and framing effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics and codes of conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethics and standards (Broadcast · Chequebook · Churnalism · Codes of ethics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to professional codes of ethics; avoid pay-for-play ('chequebook') reporting and churnalism (recycling press materials without verification); ethical practice includes source protection, transparency, and editorial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing standards: fact-checking, corrections, spiking
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing (Copy editing · Corrections · Fact-checking · Spiking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain rigorous copy-editing and fact-checking procedures; issue corrections when necessary; understand 'spiking' (withholding) as an editorial decision and ensure such decisions follow standards of accuracy and public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of sensationalism / yellow journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Fake news (Yellow Journalism) — avoid misleading or false content and attention-grabbing sensationalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not prioritize attention-grabbing over accuracy; yellow journalism aims to gather attention often at the expense of truth — broadcast journalists should guard against spreading misleading 'fake news'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television stylistic norms: visuals, soundbites, and fast cuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Television is dominated by attractive visuals (including beauty, action, and shock), with short soundbites and fast 'cuts'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TV packages should use compelling visuals, concise soundbites, and editing that maintains pacing, while balancing visual appeal against substance and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live coverage and breaking-news timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Instantaneous/live coverage of major events; breaking news expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcast outlets are expected to provide timely, often live coverage of major events; this requires rapid newsgathering, verification practices suited to live reporting, and preparedness for real-time updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory and public-interest obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Public-interest requirements enforced by regulators (e.g., FCC in U.S.; CRTC in Canada) and licence requirements to offer locally produced newscasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stations must comply with legal/regulatory obligations (licensing, public‑interest programming, local content requirements) which shape what and how news is produced and broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local newscast scheduling and output norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical local TV stations broadcast local news multiple times a day (commonly at morning, noon, early evening, and late night); stations vary in number and length of local newscasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programming decisions (frequency/timing/length of newscasts) reflect market expectations and regulatory contexts; producers should plan staffing and formats to meet these norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsroom roles and responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of roles: News anchors serve as masters-of-ceremonies reading teleprompters; meteorologists present weather using chroma key; reporters research/write stories and produce packages; videographers handle camera and live shots; segment producers choose, research and write stories and decide timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear division of labor and role expectations (anchors, reporters, producers, videographers, technical staff) are standards for producing coherent, timely broadcasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production and technical standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Newscast director assigns camera/talent positions and selects camera shots; technical director operates the video switcher; graphics operator produces lower thirds and full-screen graphics; audio technician manages microphones and mixing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical production roles should ensure broadcast-quality video/audio, appropriate graphics (lower thirds, tickers), and coordinated live switching for professional presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: All-news radio formatting norms
rubrics_metrics.description: AM radio stations often air a 6½-minute newscast at the top of the hour; some stations air shorter capsules during drive times; FM stations usually carry abbreviated forecasts or minute-long news capsules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Radio news format follows strict timing conventions (top/bottom of hour formats, drive-time briefings) requiring disciplined scripting and pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of specialized newsgathering technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically and presently, the use of videotape, satellites, airborne newsgathering (telecopters), remote units and newsgathering vehicles is standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt appropriate technologies (satellite trucks, helicopters, remote units) for live/field coverage while weighing cost, safety, and editorial value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence and cross-platform publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Convergence is sharing and cross-promoting content across media; broadcast journalists frequently also write text stories for the Web, accompanied by graphics and sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare multi-platform content: write concise web text to accompany video/audio, embed interactive elements, and cross-promote to leverage online interactivity and audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizen journalism: sourcing and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizen broadcast journalism allows civilians to post stories via Snapchat, Facebook, Twitter; news companies sometimes employ citizen journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using citizen-sourced content, apply verification, attribution, and ethical considerations equivalent to professional sourcing to avoid errors or exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branding and titling for audience recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Stations commonly use umbrella titles or catchy newscast names (e.g., 'Eyewitness News', 'Action News', 'NewsChannel 4', 'Good Morning [city]') to set themselves apart and aid Nielsen recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent branding and show titles serve programming strategy and audience measurement; choose names that support station identity and recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cable news programming differences
rubrics_metrics.description: 24-hour cable channels focus on round-the-clock current events but often fill late/prime hours with talk programs, documentaries, and specialty programming rather than continuous hard-news bulletins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cable outlets should balance rolling updates with analysis/talk formats and schedule programming to match audience expectations while maintaining factual standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education and professional preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Education is commonly required: a bachelor's degree in journalism, broadcast journalism, or interactive media; much training is hands-on via internships and campus broadcasting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional preparation combines formal education (journalism fundamentals) with internships and practical experience (EFP, editing, on-air practice) to meet industry expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety, legal, and source-protection principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Topics include freedom of information, freedom of the press, defamation, safety, and source protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists must balance legal risks (defamation), protect sources when necessary, and consider personal and team safety when reporting in hazardous or hostile environments.
